sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Encryption in transit is the practice of encrypting data as it moves across a network — between client and server, between microservices, between regions, between an application and its database — using TLS (Transport Layer Security, the successor to SSL) so that an observer on the path (a coffee-shop Wi-Fi snooper, a compromised router, an ISP, a nation-state) cannot read, tamper with, or replay the traffic.

Encryption in transit exists because networks are not private. The internet is a chain of routers, switches, fiber links, and caches operated by dozens of parties — your ISP, transit providers, the destination's ISP, CDNs, and any party that has compromised a router along the path. Any of them can read plaintext traffic in flight, modify it, or replay it. The classic demonstration is Firesheep (2010), a Firefox extension that sniffed unencrypted HTTP cookies on coffee-shop Wi-Fi and let anyone take over your Facebook or Twitter session with one click. The response was universal TLS adoption: by 2024, more than 95% of web traffic is HTTPS, Let's Encrypt has issued more than a billion free certificates, and browsers flag any non-HTTPS site as "Not Secure." TLS is so universal that plaintext HTTP on the public internet is now considered a security defect, not a default.

TLS (currently version 1.3, defined in RFC 8446, 2018) is the protocol that makes this work. The TLS handshake is the key piece: the client and server negotiate a cipher suite, authenticate the server using its certificate (which chains to a trusted Certificate Authority), exchange key material to derive a shared session key, and then encrypt all subsequent application data with that key using an authenticated cipher (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 in TLS 1.3). The handshake is asymmetric crypto (used to authenticate and establish the session key) and the data is symmetric crypto (used for bulk encryption because it is fast). TLS 1.3 reduced the handshake from two round-trips to one, dropped weak algorithms (RC4, MD5, SHA-1, static RSA key exchange), and made forward secrecy mandatory — every session uses an ephemeral key (ECDHE) that is destroyed after the session, so a future compromise of the server's long-term private key cannot decrypt past recorded traffic. This is a critical property: even if someone has been recording all your TLS traffic for years and later steals your private key, they still cannot decrypt the old traffic because the session keys are gone.

Real-world deployments span several patterns. **Public web HTTPS** is the most common: the server presents a certificate signed by a public CA (Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, Sectigo), the browser validates the chain, and traffic flows encrypted. Let's Encrypt (launched 2015) made certificates free and automated via the ACME protocol, which is why HTTPS adoption went from ~30% in 2015 to ~95% in 2024 — the cost and operational barrier disappeared. **CDN-fronted TLS** (Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS CloudFront) terminates TLS at the edge node closest to the user, then either re-encrypts to the origin (full TLS) or sends plaintext to the origin over a private link (TLS termination at edge). Cloudflare alone terminates TLS for ~20% of the web. **Service-to-service mTLS** (mutual TLS) goes further: both sides present certificates, so the server authenticates the client in addition to the client authenticating the server. Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect, and AWS App Mesh implement mTLS transparently via sidecar proxies — every service-to-service call inside the mesh is automatically encrypted with rotating certificates issued by the mesh's internal CA, without the application code being aware. This is how a microservices architecture can have every internal call encrypted without each service implementing TLS itself.

The trade-off in TLS deployment is where to terminate it. **Edge termination** (at the CDN or load balancer) means TLS is decrypted at the edge and traffic flows plaintext to the backend — this is simple and lets the LB inspect and route on HTTP headers, but it means plaintext crosses the internal network, which is unacceptable for sensitive traffic. **Backend termination** (TLS all the way to the application) means the LB operates in TCP mode and passes encrypted bytes through — this is more secure but the LB cannot route on HTTP headers and cannot do L7 health checks. The common compromise is **two-tier TLS**: TLS terminates at the LB (for header-based routing and WAF inspection), then re-encrypts to the backend over a second TLS connection — the internal segment is encrypted even though it crosses the internal network. Cloud providers charge for this (AWS NLB charges per LCU for TLS processing), and the extra hop adds ~1-2 ms of latency, but the security gain is worth it for sensitive workloads. Inside a service mesh, mTLS is automatic and free — the sidecars handle it without the application's knowledge.

Certificate management is the operational pain point. Every TLS endpoint needs a certificate, every certificate has an expiry (Let's Encrypt certs are 90 days; most others are 1-2 years; the industry is moving to shorter lifetimes), and an expired certificate means an outage — and outages from expired certs are common (Equifax 2018, Epic Games 2020, numerous internal incidents at every large company). The solution is automation: ACME (RFC 8555, 2019) is the standard protocol for certificate issuance and renewal, supported by Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, DigiCert, and most CAs. cert-manager (for Kubernetes) and AWS Certificate Manager (for AWS) automate issuance and renewal: they request a certificate, prove domain ownership via DNS-01 or HTTP-01 challenge, install the certificate on the load balancer or ingress, and renew it before expiry without human intervention. For internal mTLS, the service mesh's CA (Istio's `istiod`, Linkerd's `identity` service) issues short-lived certificates (often 24 hours) to each workload, rotates them automatically, and revokes via SPIFFE identity. The pattern across all of these: short-lived certificates, automated renewal, no human in the loop — because humans forget and outages follow.

The performance story is favorable. TLS 1.3's one-round-trip handshake adds ~10-50 ms on first connection (depending on network RTT), and TLS session resumption (via session tickets or PSK) makes subsequent connections zero-round-trip (0-RTT) on supported clients. The bulk encryption cost is negligible thanks to AES-NI (5-10 GB/s per core), and TLS records add ~20-40 bytes per record of overhead. For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the connection is multiplexed, so the handshake cost is amortized across many requests. Cloudflare and Google have measured TLS overhead at <1% of total request latency in practice. The remaining performance concerns are certificate chain validation (the client must fetch and verify intermediate certificates, which can add latency if not served by the server) and OCSP stapling (the server must prove the certificate is not revoked, which without stapling requires an extra round-trip to the CA's OCSP responder). Both are solved by proper server configuration: serve the full chain, enable OCSP stapling, use session resumption.

Finally, encryption in transit is necessary but not sufficient, just like encryption at rest. It protects against network observers but not against a compromised endpoint (if the server is owned, the attacker sees plaintext before it is encrypted). It protects against tampering in flight but not against a malicious server presenting a valid certificate (the CA system has been compromised repeatedly — Symantec in 2017, Comodo in 2011, DigiNotar in 2011, which led to the demise of DigiNotar). The defenses are layered: HTTPS for the network, certificate transparency (RFC 9162) to detect mis-issued certificates, HSTS and certificate pinning (deprecated but historically used) to prevent downgrade attacks, mTLS for service-to-service authentication, and end-to-end encryption for the highest-assurance cases (the application encrypts the payload before it hits TLS, so even the server cannot read it without a separate key — this is how end-to-end encrypted messaging works). Encryption in transit is the floor — every system must have it — but it is one layer of a defense-in-depth strategy.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant S as Server participant CA as Certificate Authority Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 Handshake (1 round-trip) C->>S: ClientHello (supported ciphers, key share, SNI) S->>S: Select cipher suite + curve S->>C: ServerHello (chosen cipher, key share) S->>C: Certificate (server cert chain) S->>C: CertificateVerify (signature over handshake with priv key) S->>C: Finished (MAC over handshake) Note over C: Verify cert chain to CA
Verify signature (server has priv key)
Derive shared secret via ECDHE C->>S: Finished (MAC over handshake) Note over C,S: Both derive same session key from ECDHE C->>S: Application data (AES-GCM with session key) S->>C: Application data (AES-GCM with session key) Note over S,CA: Cert issuance (out of band, ACME) S->>CA: CSR + domain ownership proof (DNS-01) CA->>S: Signed certificate (90 days, Let's Encrypt) ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` TLS 1.3 HANDSHAKE (1 RTT) ========================== Client Server | | | ---- ClientHello -----------------> | ciphers, key_share, SNI | | | <--- ServerHello ----------------- | chosen cipher, key_share | <--- Certificate ----------------- | server cert chain | <--- CertificateVerify ----------- | sig with priv key | <--- Finished -------------------- | MAC over handshake | | | [verify cert chain to CA] | | [verify sig: server has priv key] | | [derive session key via ECDHE] | | | | ---- Finished --------------------> | MAC over handshake | | | === encrypted app data ===========> | AES-GCM with session key | <== encrypted app data ============ | | | CERT LIFECYCLE (ACME automation): cert-manager -> CA: CSR + DNS-01 proof CA -> cert-manager: signed cert (90d) cert-manager -> LB/ingress: install cert cert-manager: renew at day 60 (no human) mTLS in service mesh: svcA -> sidecarA --[mTLS]--> sidecarB -> svcB sidecars: cert from mesh CA, 24h lifetime, auto-rotate svcA and svcB unaware of TLS (no code changes) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. The client sends a `ClientHello` listing the cipher suites and TLS versions it supports, an ephemeral key share for key agreement (ECDHE), and the SNI (Server Name Indication) telling the server which hostname it wants — this lets a single IP serve many certificates. 2. The server picks a cipher suite and curve, sends its `ServerHello` with the chosen parameters and its own ephemeral key share, then sends its certificate chain (server cert + intermediate CA cert), a `CertificateVerify` signature proving it holds the private key, and a `Finished` message containing a MAC over the entire handshake so far. 3. The client validates the certificate chain to a trusted root CA (built into the OS or browser), checks the hostname matches the SNI, checks the cert's expiry and revocation status (via OCSP stapling or CRL), verifies the `CertificateVerify` signature to confirm the server holds the private key, and combines the two ephemeral key shares via ECDHE to derive the shared session key — neither side ever transmits the session key. 4. The client sends its `Finished` message with a MAC over the handshake, and both sides now have the same session key; from this point, all application data is encrypted with an authenticated cipher (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) using keys derived from the session key. 5. On subsequent connections, the client can present a session ticket (from the previous connection) to enable 0-RTT resumption: the client sends application data in its first flight, before the server has even responded, at the cost of some replay-protection caveats. 6. The server's certificate is renewed out of band by an ACME client (cert-manager, AWS ACM): the client proves domain ownership via DNS-01 or HTTP-01 challenge, the CA signs a new short-lived certificate, and the client installs it on the load balancer or ingress automatically — no human in the loop, no outages from expired certs.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Mock TLS 1.3 handshake state machine (illustrative).
# Real TLS is implemented in OpenSSL, BoringSSL, rustls, etc.
import os, hashlib, hmac, time
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import (
    X25519PrivateKey, X25519PublicKey)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import (
    Ed25519PrivateKey, Ed25519PublicKey)
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization, hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

# --- CA (mock) ---
class CA:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.priv = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()
        self.pub = self.priv.public_key()

    def sign_cert(self, subject: str, server_pub: Ed25519PublicKey):
        cert = {"subject": subject, "issuer": self.name,
                "pub": server_pub, "not_before": int(time.time()),
                "not_after": int(time.time()) + 86400 * 90}
        sig = self.priv.sign(_cert_bytes(cert))
        return {"cert": cert, "sig": sig, "ca_pub": self.pub}

def _cert_bytes(c):
    return f"{c['subject']}|{c['issuer']}|{c['not_before']}|{c['not_after']}".encode()

# --- Server ---
class TLSServer:
    def __init__(self, hostname: str, ca: CA):
        self.hostname = hostname
        self.priv = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()       # long-term identity
        self.ephemeral = X25519PrivateKey.generate()   # per-handshake
        self.cert = ca.sign_cert(hostname, self.priv.public_key())

    def hello(self, client_hello):
        # In real TLS: pick cipher, send cert, sign handshake, send Finished
        return {"server_hello": {"cipher": "AES_256_GCM_SHA384"},
                "cert": self.cert,
                "key_share": self.ephemeral.public_key(),
                "sig": self.priv.sign(b"handshake-tbs")}

# --- Client ---
class TLSClient:
    def __init__(self, ca_pub: Ed25519PublicKey):
        self.ca_pub = ca_pub
        self.ephemeral = X25519PrivateKey.generate()

    def connect(self, server: TLSServer, hostname: str):
        ch = {"sni": hostname, "key_share": self.ephemeral.public_key(),
              "ciphers": ["AES_256_GCM_SHA384"]}
        sh = server.hello(ch)

        # 1. verify cert chain -> CA
        cert = sh["cert"]["cert"]
        assert cert["issuer"] != cert["subject"]      # not self-signed
        assert cert["subject"] == hostname            # SNI match
        assert cert["not_before"] <= time.time() <= cert["not_after"]
        sh["cert"]["ca_pub"].verify(sh["cert"]["sig"], _cert_bytes(cert))

        # 2. verify server signature (proves possession of priv key)
        server.priv.public_key().verify(sh["sig"], b"handshake-tbs")

        # 3. ECDHE -> derive shared secret (session key)
        shared = self.ephemeral.exchange(sh["key_share"])
        session_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32,
                           salt=None, info=b"tls13 derived").derive(shared)

        # 4. encrypt application data
        cipher = AESGCM(session_key)
        return {"cipher": cipher, "server": server.hostname}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ca = CA("MyRootCA")
    server = TLSServer("api.example.com", ca)
    client = TLSClient(ca.pub)
    session = client.connect(server, "api.example.com")
    ct = session["cipher"].encrypt(os.urandom(12), b"GET /balance",
                                    session["server"].encode())
    print("encrypted app data (hex):", ct[:16].hex(), "...")
    print("decrypted:", session["cipher"].decrypt(ct[:12], ct[12:],
                                                  session["server"].encode()))
```

quiz.explanation: Mutual TLS is TLS where both sides present and validate certificates — the server authenticates the client in addition to the client authenticating the server. In standard one-way TLS (used for public HTTPS), only the server presents a certificate; the client is authenticated at the application layer (cookie, API key, OAuth token) after the TLS session is established.

quiz.explanation: Certificate transparency (RFC 9162) is a public, append-only log of every certificate issued by participating CAs. When a CA issues a certificate, it must submit the certificate (or a "pre-certificate") to at least two CT logs, which return signed timestamps (SCTs) that the server includes in its TLS handshake. Browsers refuse to trust certificates without SCTs, which forces CAs to log everything.
